title: Ezekiel 10:1–8
context: Ezekiel 10:1–8 continues the prophet’s account. Above the cherubim appears something like a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne (10:1; compare 1:26); the stone rendered sapphire may also be lapis lazuli. The LORD tells the man clothed in linen to go in between the whirling wheels, under the cherub, fill his hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city (10:2). The significance of the coals is not explained; readers commonly take them as fire of judgment on Jerusalem, and some compare Revelation 8:5, while the coal of Isaiah 6:6–7 cleanses rather than judges; these passages are named without harmonizing. The cloud fills the inner court, and the LORD’s glory mounts up from the cherub and stands over the threshold of the house, which is filled with the cloud and the brightness of the glory (10:3–4; compare 9:3; 1 Kings 8:10–11; Exodus 40:34). The sound of the cherubim’s wings is like “the voice of God Almighty when he speaks” (10:5; compare 1:24). A cherub hands fire to the man in linen, and the form of a man’s hand is seen under their wings (10:6–8). Both traditions read the scene as shared ground, holding that the holy presence that once filled the house now prepares to judge the city and to leave the temple.

verses.text: Then I looked, and see, in the expanse that was over the head of the cherubim there appeared above them as it were a sapphire stone, as the appearance of the likeness of a throne.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel saw above the cherubim something like a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne. Arminian readers note the echo of 1:26, named without harmonizing, and they see the same throne of God present in the vision of judgment as in the vision of the prophet’s call by the river.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that the stone rendered sapphire may also be lapis lazuli. They read the throne as the sign of God’s sovereign rule even as judgment falls, and they treat the description as shared ground on God’s majesty.

verses.text: He spoke to the man clothed in linen, and said, “Go in between the whirling wheels, even under the cherub, and fill both your hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city.” He went in as I watched.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the man in linen to fill his hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. Arminian readers note that the coals are commonly taken as fire of judgment, though their significance is not explained, and they hold the reading loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reading and compare Revelation 8:5, while observing that the coal of Isaiah 6:6–7 cleanses rather than judges; these are named without harmonizing. They read the verse as showing that the fire of judgment comes from the very presence of God.

verses.text: Now the cherubim stood on the right side of the house when the man went in; and the cloud filled the inner court.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim stood on the right side of the house when the man went in, and the cloud filled the inner court. Arminian readers note that the cloud recalls the LORD’s presence in the tabernacle and temple, and they see the same presence that once blessed now preparing to judge and depart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that the right side may mean the south side of the house, though the detail is not explained. They read the cloud as a sign of the holy presence, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD’s glory mounted up from the cherub, and stood over the threshold of the house; and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was full of the brightness of the LORD’s glory.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s glory mounted up from the cherub and stood over the threshold of the house, which was filled with the cloud and brightness. Arminian readers note the repetition of 9:3, named without harmonizing, and they see the glory pausing at the threshold before leaving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same movement and compare 1 Kings 8:10–11, where “the cloud filled the LORD’s house” at its dedication, and Exodus 40:34. They read the scene as a solemn reversal of the temple’s dedication, and both traditions see it as shared ground.

verses.text: The sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard even to the outer court, as the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.
verses.arminianNotes: The sound of the cherubim’s wings was heard to the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks. Arminian readers note the echo of 1:24, “like the voice of the Almighty”, named without harmonizing, and they see the overwhelming majesty of God’s presence in the vision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the sound as conveying the power of the presence that is about to leave the temple. They observe that the cherubim’s movement is linked to God’s speaking, a detail that both traditions read as underscoring divine authority.

verses.text: It came to pass, when he commanded the man clothed in linen, saying, “Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim,” that he went in and stood beside a wheel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commanded the man clothed in linen to take fire from between the whirling wheels, and he went in and stood beside a wheel. Arminian readers note the man’s obedience in approaching the holy place, and they see the scene as the outworking of the command given in 10:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same obedience and the repetition of the command, which emphasizes that the judgment comes from God. They observe that the term whirling wheels is introduced here and in 10:13, and they read it as part of the vision’s link with chapter 1.

verses.text: The cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it, and put it into the hands of him who was clothed in linen, who took it and went out.
verses.arminianNotes: A cherub stretched out his hand to the fire between the cherubim and put some into the hands of the man in linen, who took it and went out. Arminian readers note that the fire is handed over by a cherub, and they see the judgment carried out in an orderly way under God’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same detail and observe that the narrative does not describe the scattering of the coals over the city. They read the verse as showing that judgment proceeds from God’s presence through his appointed agents, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: The form of a man’s hand appeared here in the cherubim under their wings.
verses.arminianNotes: The form of a man’s hand appeared in the cherubim under their wings. Arminian readers note that this detail echoes the hands of the living creatures in 1:8, though they do not harmonize the descriptions, and they see the vision emphasizing that the cherubim can act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the detail as preparing for the fuller description of the cherubim that follows. They observe that the prophet’s careful attention to such details reflects his priestly concern with the holy things of the temple.
